title: Another softening: ‘God’s law’ often means only precepts binding under mortal
source_text: XXVI. Alii notant peccatum veniale non dici simpliciter esse contra Dei legem, quia per legem Dei intelliguntur communiter praecepta obligantia sub mortali, & quorum observatio necessaria est ad salutem, juxta illud, Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata. Concedunt tamen aliquo sensu verum esse quod peccatum veniale sit contra legem, quia generatim omne peccatum est praevaricatio legis: ac praeterea quia dubitari non potest, quin peccatum veniale repugnet rectae rationi, quae est quaedam in nobis impressio divinae legis. Ista Petrus a Sancto Joseph, in Idea Theologiae Moralis, lib. 2. cap. 3. Resolutione 5.
pass_a_gloss: Others note that venial sin is not said simply to be against God’s law, because by God’s law are commonly understood precepts binding under mortal guilt, and whose observance is necessary unto salvation, according to that word, If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. Yet they grant that in some sense it is true that venial sin is against the law, because in general every sin is a transgression of the law; and besides because it cannot be doubted that venial sin fights against right reason, which is a certain impression of the divine law in us. So Peter of Saint Joseph, in the Idea of Moral Theology, book 2, chapter 3, Resolution 5.
pass_b_english: Some reserve ‘God’s law’ for precepts binding under mortal and needful for salvation—hence venial is not ‘simply’ against that law.
They still admit every sin transgresses law broadly, and venial wars with right reason as law’s imprint.
